name: Arugula
tile_uses: The salad, pasta, rice bowls, on top of anything
why_now: Arugula is a cool-weather green. In summer heat it bolts and turns harsh; planted in September, it's ready in October with a gentler, peppery bite. It's the first green in months that tastes like it wanted to grow.
how_to_choose: Bunches with small leaves are milder than big, deeply lobed ones
No wet or slimy leaves at the bottom of the bag
Bunched arugula from a market usually tastes more of itself than the washed clamshells
buy_this_much: 2 bunches, or one big bag. Buy it twice a week if you can — it doesn't keep like the rest of this basket.
price_note: Farmers market bunches are often cheaper per ounce than clamshells, and taste better.

flavor_paths.name: Raw, dressed last
flavor_paths.description: Olive oil, lemon, salt, right before eating. The default.

flavor_paths.name: Wilted
flavor_paths.description: Tossed into hot pasta off the heat. It collapses in seconds.

flavor_paths.name: As a topping
flavor_paths.description: A handful on anything warm, undressed.

weekday_uses: Wilted into pasta with lemon and parmesan
On top of a fried egg on toast
weekend_use: The base of the October salad: arugula, Asian pear, pomegranate, and torn dates, dressed at the last second.
storage: Unwashed, wrapped in a dry paper towel inside a bag, in the crisper. Three or four days. Wash it right before using.
one_thing_to_learn: Dress greens at the last possible moment. Salt pulls water out of leaves, and oil weighs them down, so a salad dressed ten minutes early is a wilted salad. Put everything in the bowl, carry it to the table, and toss it there.
